title: På legekontoret / At the Doctor's Office
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, you often use the verb 'å være' (to be) to describe health conditions, e.g., 'Jeg er syk' (I am sick). Additionally, Norwegian speakers tend to be more direct in medical conversations, so phrases like 'Jeg har vondt i hodet' (I have a headache) are common. Be cautious with false friends like 'lege' (doctor), which is not related to the English 'leg'.
rule: When discussing health at the doctor's office, use the present tense for current conditions and the past tense for describing symptoms. The verb 'å ha' (to have) is used for ailments, e.g., 'Jeg har feber' (I have a fever). Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe, e.g., 'en varm panna' (a warm forehead) vs. 'et kaldt rom' (a cold room).

title: Å bestille overnatting / Booking Accommodation
bridge: In Norwegian, the verb 'å bestille' is used for booking accommodation, similar to 'to book' in English. However, Norwegian often uses the preposition 'på' (at) instead of 'a' (a/an) when specifying the type of accommodation, which might feel unnatural to English speakers. Additionally, Norwegian speakers tend to be more direct in their requests, so phrases like 'Kan jeg få...' (Can I get...) are common, whereas English speakers might use more polite phrasing like 'Could I have...'.
rule: To book accommodation in Norwegian, use the structure: 'Kan jeg bestille [type of accommodation] på [location]?' For example, 'Kan jeg bestille et hotellrom på Oslo?' (Can I book a hotel room in Oslo?). The verb 'å bestille' is regular and follows standard conjugation patterns. Remember to use the correct definite form for the type of accommodation when specifying a particular place, e.g., 'hotellrommet' (the hotel room).

title: Å veksle penger / Exchanging Money
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, the verb 'å veksle' (to exchange) is used for both exchanging currency and changing money. Be careful not to confuse it with 'å skifte' (to change), which is used for changing clothes or behavior. Additionally, Norwegian uses the word 'kontor' for 'office', which is similar to English, but 'bank' remains the same in both languages.
rule: To talk about exchanging money in Norwegian, use the verb 'å veksle' followed by the object. For example, 'Jeg vil veksle penger' (I want to exchange money). When specifying the currency, use the preposition 'til' (to). For instance, 'veksle til norske kroner' (exchange to Norwegian kroner). Remember that Norwegian word order is generally Subject-Verb-Object, similar to English.

title: Å snakke om arbeidserfaring / Talking About Work Experience
bridge: In Norwegian, when discussing work experience, the verb 'å ha' (to have) is often used to describe the duration of employment, similar to English. However, Norwegian typically places the time period after the verb, unlike English where it often comes before. Additionally, Norwegian uses the preposition 'i' (in) to indicate the company or field, whereas English uses 'at' or 'in'. Be cautious with word order and prepositions to avoid common mistakes.
rule: To talk about work experience in Norwegian, use the structure: 'Jeg har jobbet i [company/field] i [time period].' For example, 'Jeg har jobbet i IT-bransjen i tre år.' (I have worked in the IT industry for three years.) The verb 'å ha jobbet' is the perfect tense of 'å jobbe' (to work), and the time period always follows 'i'. Remember to use the correct preposition 'i' for both the company/field and the time period.

title: På postkontoret / At the Post Office
bridge: In Norwegian, unlike English, the word for 'post office' is 'postkontor', which directly translates to 'post office'. However, when asking for services, Norwegians often use more specific verbs like 'å sende' (to send) instead of just 'send' as in English. Be cautious with false friends like 'pakke' (package) which is pronounced similarly to the English 'pack' but means something different.
rule: To talk about postal services in Norwegian, use the verb 'å sende' for sending items. The noun 'postkontor' is used for 'post office'. Common phrases include 'Kan jeg få...?' (Can I get...?) for requesting services. Remember that Norwegian word order is similar to English in questions, but adjectives often come after the noun, e.g., 'en stor pakke' (a big package).

title: Leie en leilighet / Renting a flat
bridge: In Norwegian, the verb 'å leie' is used for renting, similar to 'to rent' in English. However, Norwegian uses the preposition 'på' to indicate the place where you rent, unlike English which uses 'from'. Be careful not to directly translate 'rent from' as 'leie fra', as this is incorrect in Norwegian.
rule: To talk about renting a flat in Norwegian, use the structure 'Jeg leier en leilighet på [location]'. The verb 'å leie' is irregular and its present tense forms are: jeg leier, du leier, han/hun/den leier, vi leier, dere leier, de leier. Remember to use the correct preposition 'på' when specifying the location.

title: Å presentere seg / Introducing Yourself
bridge: In Norwegian, introducing yourself often includes your first name and surname, unlike in English where just the first name is common. Norwegians also frequently mention their profession or where they are from, which is less typical in casual English introductions. Be aware that Norwegian names can have unique pronunciations, so listen carefully and don’t hesitate to ask for repetition.
rule: When introducing yourself in Norwegian, use the phrase 'Hei, jeg heter [name]' (Hi, my name is [name]). If you want to include more information, you can add 'Jeg er [profession]' (I am [profession]) or 'Jeg kommer fra [place]' (I come from [place]). The verb 'å hete' (to be named) is used for your name, and 'å være' (to be) is used for profession or origin. Remember to use the correct pronunciation of Norwegian names, as they often differ from English.

title: Å klage og be om unnskyldning / Complaining and Apologizing
bridge: In Norwegian, complaining and apologizing often involve more direct expressions compared to English. While English speakers might use indirect phrases like 'I’m sorry for the inconvenience,' Norwegians tend to be more straightforward, saying 'Jeg beklager' (I regret). Additionally, Norwegians often use 'Unnskyld' (Excuse me) to get attention, similar to 'Sorry' in English, but it’s less apologetic and more functional. Be cautious not to overuse 'Beklager' (Sorry) as it can sound overly formal in casual settings.
rule: To complain, use 'Jeg er lei meg over...' (I am upset about...) or 'Det er ikke bra' (That’s not good). For apologies, 'Jeg beklager' (I regret) is formal, while 'Unnskyld' (Excuse me) is informal. Note that 'Unnskyld' can also mean 'Pardon me' when asking for attention. Always match the formality level to the context. In casual settings, 'Beklager' (Sorry) is common but less sincere than 'Jeg beklager.'

title: Min hjemby / My Hometown
bridge: In Norwegian, describing your hometown often involves using the verb 'å være' (to be) in a more static sense compared to English, where we might use more dynamic verbs. Norwegian also uses the preposition 'i' for 'in' a city, but 'på' for 'in' smaller towns or villages, which can be confusing for English speakers. Additionally, Norwegian adjectives often come after the noun, unlike in English where they typically precede the noun.
rule: To describe your hometown in Norwegian, use the structure 'Jeg bor i/på [place]. [Place] er [adjective].' For example, 'Jeg bor i Oslo. Oslo er stor.' Note that 'i' is used for cities and 'på' for smaller towns or villages. Adjectives follow the noun and must agree in gender and number with the noun they describe. Common adjectives include 'stor' (big), 'liten' (small), 'vakker' (beautiful), and 'rolig' (quiet).

title: Å snakke om hobbyer / Talking about hobbies
bridge: In Norwegian, talking about hobbies often involves the verb 'å like' (to like) followed by the infinitive, similar to English. However, Norwegians frequently use the preposition 'å' before the activity, which doesn't exist in English. Be careful not to directly translate 'I like to read' as 'Jeg liker å lese' is correct, but 'Jeg liker lese' is not. Also, Norwegians often use the present tense to describe hobbies, even when talking about general preferences.
rule: To talk about hobbies in Norwegian, use the structure 'Jeg liker å [infinitive verb]'. For example, 'Jeg liker å lese' (I like to read). The verb 'å like' is followed by the infinitive form of the verb, which is the same as the dictionary form. Remember to use the correct article 'å' before the activity. For negative statements, use 'Jeg liker ikke å [infinitive verb]', such as 'Jeg liker ikke å se på TV' (I don't like to watch TV).
